opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it was a mix of the people, the place, and the timing.

Before NYU I spent several years at FAIR, Facebook AI Research, and I really loved that environment. It was open, research-driven, and full of very smart people working on fundamental problems. But at some point I started thinking about what I wanted for the next phase. In industry you can do amazing work, but I felt that being a professor gave me a different kind of freedom. You can work with students over many years, watch them grow, and pursue directions that don't have to justify themselves on a product roadmap. That long-term, slightly riskier kind of research really appealed to me.

As for NYU specifically, the AI community there is unusual. Yann LeCun is there, and there's a long tradition of people who believed in neural networks and representation learning long before it was fashionable. The Courant Institute and the Center for Data Science bring together people from computer science, math, and neuroscience, so you get a lot of cross-pollination. For someone like me who works on visual representation learning and is increasingly interested in how vision connects to language, world models, and more general intelligence, that's a great fit.

And then there's New York itself. It's not a typical college town. It's dense, energetic, very international, and you're constantly running into people from finance, media, art, and startups. I like that tension. It keeps you from living only in a research bubble. Plenty of AI researchers end up in the Bay Area, which makes sense, but I think there's value in being somewhere a little different, where you're forced to think about how this technology meets the rest of the world.

So it felt like the right combination: academic freedom, a strong and somewhat contrarian research tradition, and a city that keeps you curious.

r001.rationale: The response cites NYU’s research community, academic freedom, and New York’s energy, but does not mention a connection to filmmakers Xie admires.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a few things came together at once. Before NYU I had spent a long time on the West Coast — grad school at UC San Diego, then several years at Facebook AI Research in the Bay Area. I loved that period, but I started to feel I wanted a change of environment, and I wanted to go back to academia, to work with students and build my own group.

New York was appealing for reasons that are partly personal and partly professional. On the professional side, NYU has a very special tradition in deep learning. Yann LeCun has been there for a long time, and Courant and the Center for Data Science have this culture where people think about the fundamentals of representation learning quite seriously, not just chasing the next benchmark. When I visited, I felt the conversations I was having were the kind I wanted to be having for the next decade. Also, New York has become a real center for AI — there's a dense concentration of labs, companies, and people passing through, so you never feel isolated from what's happening in industry even though you're in a university.

On the personal side, I just like the city. I grew up in China, in a big dense place, and after years in the suburbs of California, New York felt more like home in a strange way — the energy, the food, the fact that you can walk everywhere. My family also liked the idea.

And finally, I think there's something about a city that forces you to interact with people who are not in your field. In the Bay Area it's very easy to spend all your time talking to other AI researchers. In New York you're constantly bumping into artists, finance people, writers. I think that's healthy for research — it keeps you from getting too narrow about what problems matter.

r001.rationale: The response cites NYU’s deep-learning tradition and other professional and personal reasons, but does not mention a connection to filmmakers Saining Xie admires.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal was the combination of NYU and New York itself. Academically, I wanted an environment where I could exchange ideas with people working on different aspects of AI and have room to develop my own research direction. NYU felt like a good place for that.

And the city was a big part of the attraction. I like being somewhere where your life isn’t entirely contained within the university or the tech community. You encounter people with very different interests and perspectives. That combination—an intellectually stimulating university and a city with so much happening—was really appealing to me.
